context: Current closing price of Consolidated Edison (ED): $108.55 USD as of 2026-08-04.
justification_text:
My point estimates reflect a modestly bullish baseline for the asset across all three horizons, with the price drifting slightly upward from roughly 108.7 at one day out to 109.5 at one month. This gentle upward drift is consistent with a mean-reversion assumption around a near-term fair value, combined with a small positive drift term that reflects the broader macro environment at the time of the forecast. At the one-day horizon, the estimate is largely anchored to the last observed price with minimal adjustment, since very short-term forecasts are dominated by momentum and microstructure. At the one-week and one-month horizons, I incorporated expectations of modest fundamental support — likely a combination of steady economic data, central bank posture, and sector-level tailwinds — which justify a slight upward tilt rather than a flat or declining path.

The confidence interval widths widen considerably as the horizon extends, which reflects the standard square-root-of-time scaling of uncertainty in financial price models. At one day, the 90% interval spans roughly 1.8 points, capturing normal intraday-to-overnight volatility. By one week, the interval widens to 7 points, and by one month it reaches 15 points, reflecting the compounding effect of daily volatility over longer periods and the increasing probability that new fundamental information will arrive and shift the trajectory. I also factored in elevated macro uncertainty — including shifting interest rate expectations and geopolitical noise — which pushed the tails slightly wider than a pure historical volatility estimate would suggest.

There are several specific risks that could push realized outcomes outside these intervals. On the upside, a positive surprise in key economic data, a dovish pivot in central bank communication, or a sudden surge in risk appetite could push prices well above the upper bound of the one-month interval. On the downside, a credit event, an unexpected policy tightening, or a broad risk-off episode driven by geopolitical escalation could breach the lower bound. Liquidity conditions also matter — if market depth deteriorates, even modest order flow imbalances could produce outsized moves that my model, calibrated on more normal conditions, would not fully anticipate. These tail scenarios are precisely the situations where probabilistic interval forecasts tend to underperform.
